title: Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models

paper.title: Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Graph diffusion models are competitive approaches for generating complex graph-structured data. However, when such distributions have strict structural constraints, diffusion models may fail to capture them exactly, resulting in the generation of invalid graphs. In this paper, we propose a method for grounding graph diffusion models in domain-specific knowledge via First Order Logic (FOL), leveraging its expressive and interpretable formalism to impose structural constraints on the generative process. We incorporate domain knowledge using classifier guidance, a technique that conditions the diffusion model’s distribution on external variables to exert control over the sampled data. During the generative process, classifier guidance steers the denoising trajectory to optimize an objective function, which we define as a fuzzy and differentiable relaxation of the logical rules. Our methodology requires only the specification of constraints in FOL, whose satisfaction is encouraged at inference time to guide a pre-trained generative model. We evaluate our approach by comparing the unconditional generation of knowledge graphs with our logic-guided framework, which incorporates domain ontologies as structural constraints during inference. This approach significantly increases the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy the ontological constraints.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Graph generation involves learning an underlying data distribution to facilitate the synthesis of novel, realistic graph structures. Graph diffusion models ( Jo et al. 2022 ; Vignac et al. 2023 ; Huang et al. 2023 ; Cognolato et al. 2026a ; Cognolato et al. 2026b ) and flow-matching models ( Eijkelboom et al. 2024 ; Qin et al. 2024 ) can model distributions over graphs with discrete labels and continuous attributes. In some applications, such as biology, graphs need to satisfy domain-specific rules ( Rigoni et al. 2020 ) that define whether a graph is well-formed. However, neural generative models lack a mechanism to explicitly enforce structural constraints, which requires specialized techniques to tackle them. Thus, the problem of constrained graph generation, i.e., sampling graphs from a subspace of elements satisfying a set of constraints, has gained traction ( Liu et al. 2018 ; Rigoni et al. 2025 ; Madeira et al. 2024 ) . First Order Logic (FOL) ( Barwise 1977 ) may serve as a unified approach to encode and combine heterogeneous constraints. FOL can be used to formalize properties in graphs, where node and edge labels are represented as unary and binary predicates, respectively ( Cai et al. 1992 ) . The rules may act on single nodes, their neighbors, and the type or direction of the relations, e.g., bipartiteness and transitivity. FOL rules may also act considering the whole graph structure, e.g., requiring the presence of a specific node type. The ability to operate both locally and globally provides a tool for controlling the structure and content of graphs. This setup has enabled the definition of ontologies for knowledge graphs, providing a schema for otherwise unstructured data ( Gruber 1993 ) . In this paper, we propose LTN-guidance, a methodology for injecting domain knowledge as FOL constraints into the generative process of graph diffusion models ( Vignac et al. 2023 ) , without any additional training. Our aim is to increase the probability of sampling valid graphs. First, we propose a graph signature, i.e., the collection of symbols defining the vocabulary of the first order language, enabling the definition of logical formulas over labeled graphs. During generation, we use classifier guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol 2021 ) to steer a pre-trained diffusion model toward optimizing rule satisfaction (the external objective function). Our method provides the target FOL constraints as Logic Tensor Network (LTN) ( Badreddine et al. 2022 ) differentiable functions. A mechanism based on Focal Loss ( Lin et al. 2017 ) allows adaptive reweighting of constraints, increasing the contribution of less satisfied sentences in the generative process. Finally, we propose cheaper implementations of LTN functions, e.g., for implementing cardinality constraints over edges. Our main contributions are: 1. A graph signature that allows the definition of logical rules over labeled graphs. We integrate the signature with axioms to ensure label exclusivity; 2. A plug-and-play method for steering graph diffusion models with knowledge in FOL. During inference, FOL constraints are translated to differentiable functions through Logic Tensor Network, and used to steer a pretrained unconditional model with classifier guidance. 3. We evaluated a popular graph diffusion model, DiGress ( Vignac et al. 2023 ) , with and without our technique, for the generation of small knowledge graphs from the IntelliGraphs benchmark ( Thanapalasingam et al. 2023 ) against knowledge graph embedding and LLM-based approaches. We observe an improvement in validity, achieving > 95 % >95\% in most datasets. 4. We performed generation with new rules, compatible and conflicting with the data, to evaluate the conditional in-distribution and out-of-distribution validity, respectively. LTN-guidance consistently shows responsiveness to input formulas by producing a high fraction of valid graphs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first inference-time FOL constraints guidance framework for graph diffusion.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Constrained Graph Generation (CGG) can be based on deep learning or, in the specific case of FOL rules, on Weighted First Order Model Sampling (WFOMS). For deep-learning-based CGG, the application of constraints to deep graph generative models remains in its infancy, as very few works tackle the problem, or are limited to a specific class of constraints. Constrained Graph Variational Auto Encoders (CGVAE) ( Liu et al. 2018 ) and Conditional CGVAE ( Rigoni et al. 2020 ) enforce valency constraints in the molecular domain, closely related to the out-degree of nodes. The model’s generative process is autoregressive, allowing at each step to disable linking with atoms that have filled up their valency. ConStruct ( Madeira et al. 2024 ) is a diffusion model where the whole diffusion and denoising sequences remain in the constrained space, making the samples valid by design. However, the classes of constrains considered are limited to minor-hereditary properties that, if true for a graph, are also true for its minors. The generation of graphs can also be seen as the sampling of variables assignments satisfying the set of FOL rules. This has been explored in Weighted First Order Model Sampling (WFOMS) ( Wang et al. 2024 ) , closely related to Weighted First Order Model Counting (WFOMC) ( Van den Broeck et al. 2011 ) . Lifted (i.e., polynomial) sampling algorithms exist up to the C 2 C^{2} fragment of FOL ( Wang et al. 2024 ) , that is, allowing sentences with universal and counting existential quantifiers ∀ , ∃ ≥ k , ∃ ≤ k , ∃ = k \forall,\exists_{\geq k},\exists_{\leq k},\exists_{=k} with up to two variables per sentence. Although exact in its sampling, lifted WFOMS’s limitation to two variables could render it ineffective for certain applications, such as ontologies with over 3 variables ( Thanapalasingam et al. 2023 ) . Regarding Knowledge Graph (KG) generation, where FOL ontologies are usually defined, there are two prominent KG completion methods: (1) entity embedding and probabilistic link prediction ( Peng et al. 2023 ) ; (2) using Large Language Models (LLM) ( Yao et al. 2025 ) . The former is designed to predict missing links by computing the likelihood of new triples from the trained embeddings and not to generate new entities. The latter treats triples sets as a textual sequence, and new triples are generated as new tokens. However, knowledge graph embedding assumes link independence during sampling, limiting the expressiveness of the resulting graph distributions; at the same time, treating graphs as text negates the inductive biases that facilitate scalability to larger structures. Thanks to the availability of KG data and their ontologies, we will evaluate our methodology on KG generation with FOL constraints.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: We present a formal definition of labeled graphs. A labeled graph G G is a tuple G = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , Λ v , Λ e ) G=({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}},\Lambda_{v},\Lambda_{e}) where 𝒱 {\mathcal{V}} is the set of nodes, ℰ ⊆ 𝒱 × 𝒱 {\mathcal{E}}\subseteq{\mathcal{V}}\times{\mathcal{V}} is the set of edges, Λ v : 𝒱 → ℒ v \Lambda_{v}:{\mathcal{V}}\to{\mathcal{L}}_{v} and Λ e : ℰ → ℒ e \Lambda_{e}:{\mathcal{E}}\to{\mathcal{L}}_{e} are the node and edge labeling functions, where ℒ v {\mathcal{L}}_{v} and ℒ e {\mathcal{L}}_{e} are the node and edge labels, respectively. sections.heading: 3.1 Diffusion Models for Graphs
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al. 2020 ; Austin et al. 2021 ) are a class of generative models where the objective is to learn an approximation p θ ​ ( G ) p_{\theta}(G) with parameters θ \theta of an unknown data distribution q ⁡ ( G ) q(G) . DDPMs achieve this as a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) process, reaching convergence to the learned distribution after a certain amount of Markov transitions. Diffusion models for graphs ( Vignac et al. 2023 ) jointly generate nodes, edges, and their labels. Two discrete diffusion processes ( Austin et al. 2021 ) randomly flip node and edge labels in 𝑿 {\bm{X}} and 𝑬 {\bm{E}} , potentially removing or adding connectivity, proceeding from time t = 0 t=0 to t = T t=T . sections.heading: 3.2 First Order Logic
sections.text: First Order Logic (FOL) deals with the formalization of facts, which can be either true or false. FOL operates on a first order language, described by a signature : Σ = ( 𝒞 , ℱ , 𝒫 ) , \Sigma=({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{F}},{\mathcal{P}}), (3) where 𝒞 {\mathcal{C}} is a set of constant symbols, ℱ {\mathcal{F}} is a set of function symbols, and 𝒫 {\mathcal{P}} is a set of predicate symbols. An interpretation ℐ {\mathcal{I}} over Σ \Sigma maps each constant c c to a specific individual ℐ ⁡ ( c ) {\mathcal{I}}(c) in a domain of discourse 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} , function symbols f f to functions ℐ ⁡ ( f ) : 𝒟 n → 𝒟 {\mathcal{I}}(f):{\mathcal{D}}^{n}\to{\mathcal{D}} of arity n n , and predicate symbols P P to relations ℐ ⁡ ( P ) ⊆ 𝒟 n {\mathcal{I}}(P)\subseteq{\mathcal{D}}^{n} of arity n n . Formulas ϕ \phi are strings composed of variables symbols (e.g., x , y , z x,y,z ), non-logical symbols contained in the signature Σ \Sigma , and logical symbols, comprising connectives (conjunction, disjunction, negation) and quantifiers (existential and universal). The semantics of the logic defines the meaning of the logical operators. For example, classical FOL considers only truth values { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} (false and true), while fuzzy logic also considers intermediate values in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . A sentence, i.e., a formula with no unquantified variables, is satisfied by an interpretation ℐ {\mathcal{I}} if applying ℐ {\mathcal{I}} to symbols in Σ \Sigma evaluates to true given the semantics of the logic.

sections.heading: 7 Experiments
sections.text: In our experimentation, we consider three research questions: RQ1: Does LTN-guidance increase the satisfaction of dataset rules? RQ2: How does LTN-guidance affect the denoising process? RQ3: Does LTN-guidance allow the addition of new rules to either restrict the support or shift it out of distribution?

sections.heading: 7.1 Benchmark
sections.text: We use the IntelliGraphs benchmark ( Thanapalasingam et al. 2023 ) to evaluate FOL-guided graph generation. IntelliGraphs contains five Knowledge Graphs (KGs) datasets designed to test different forms of semantic validity. syn-paths tests directed path structure; syn-types tests compatibility between entity and relation types together with a fixed-cardinality constraint; and syn-tipr instantiates a time-indexed person-role ontology pattern. The two real-world datasets contain Wikidata-derived subgraphs: wd-movies describes a movie through actors, directors, and genres, whereas wd-articles describes scholarly articles and ordered authorship information. The latter is the most structurally complex because valid graphs must represent consecutive author positions without gaps. This same benchmark was used in Wang et al. (2025) , and the amount of available data is substantially larger than existing generic graph datasets ( Huang et al. 2023 ) . Graphs in the datasets are in Resource Description Framework (RDF) ( Cyganiak et al. 2014 ) format, i.e., triples 𝒯 = { ( s , r , o ) : s , o ∈ 𝒟 , r ∈ ℛ } {\mathcal{T}}=\{(s,r,o):s,o\in{\mathcal{D}},r\in{\mathcal{R}}\} where s s is the subject entity, r r the edge predicate or relation, o o the object entity, and 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} and ℛ {\mathcal{R}} are the entity and relation sets, respectively. sections.heading: 7.2 Implementation Details
sections.text: We apply LTN-guidance to DiGress ( Vignac et al. 2023 ) , a state-of-the-art graph diffusion model. Because DiGress was originally implemented for undirected graphs, we reimplemented parts of the model and Graph Transformer ( Dwivedi and Bresson 2020 ) to avoid symmetries in the adjacency matrix, e.g., removing matrix symmetrization operations 𝐀𝐀 ⊤ {\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{A}}^{\top} . This allows DiGress to be used for the generation of directed graphs. We compare DiGress against ComplEx ( Trouillon et al. 2016 ) , the best KG embedding baseline of IntelliGraphs, and ProvCreator ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , an LLM-based model. Specialized constrained generation methods are not applicable to this setup, e.g., ConStruct ( Madeira et al. 2024 ) only handles minor-hereditary properties, which do not have any overlap with the benchmark. We note that these baselines directly use the triples format, while we use their labeled graph transformation. Furthermore, ComplEx receives the correct entity set, which is not true for other methods. For our guided models, we used standard LTN values for p p , while the guidance strength was split into λ x \lambda_{x} for nodes and λ e \lambda_{e} for edges gradients, and their validity-optimizing value per dataset was found through grid search in the range [ 10 − 5 , 1 ] [10^{-5},1] . All experiments were conducted on a single A40 GPU. More details on the hyperparameter search and selected values can be found in Appendix A of the supplementary material.

sections.heading: (RQ1) Improving validity on dataset.
sections.text: We use LTN-guidance to integrate the rules used to check the validity. Our technique increases validity where the unconditional model violates constraints, while preserving near-perfect validity on the other datasets. The results are presented in Table 1 where, although some metrics and datasets might be redundant, we chose to keep them for the completeness of the benchmark. It can be seen that DiGress, even without guidance, achieves very good results in all datasets, producing practically perfect results on syn-paths and syn-tipr . In syn-types and wd-movies , we observe that unconditional DiGress is outperformed by the ProvCreator baseline. For the former, we find that the source of error is the cardinality constraint of the dataset. In fact, the validity reached by DiGress is very close to the percentage of triples set of length 10 without duplicates in the dataset. The inclusion of the cardinality constraint in Eq. 24 improves its satisfaction, leading to the very high validity of 95.70 % 95.70\% . In wd-movies , LTN-guidance also improves results over vanilla DiGress with an average validity of 97.37 % 97.37\% , outperforming ProvCreator. Still, classifier guidance did not show substantial improvements on wd-articles , the most challenging dataset. In particular, the most unsatisfied constraint entails having no gaps in the paper author positions. Near the final denoising steps, the unconditional transition becomes sharply concentrated, and the chosen guidance strength is insufficient to change the model’s predictions. Increasing the weights was insufficient, so a more complex weighting scheme is needed. Regarding distributional metrics, we observe that guidance does not substantially skew the distribution compared to the unconditional models. This means that the technique does not sacrifice sample quality for validity. sections.heading: (RQ3) Plugging new rules.
sections.text: We evaluate the capability of LTN-guidance to enforce rules not considered in the datasets in two setups: (1) support restriction, where the new rules are compatible with the current knowledge, providing an additional control signal; (2) support shift, where we introduce new conflicting rules, removing broken ones from the data rules. For example, requiring a genre for each KG in wd-movies constitutes a restriction, while changing the number of triples for syn-types to 12 is a shift, as no in-distribution KG satisfies this condition. Details on added rules can be found in Appendix B of the supplementary material. We want to remark that setup 2 is very challenging, corresponding to out-of-distribution generation, which is non-trivial for generative models. Results are shown in Fig. 3 . We observe that for the support restriction task, LTN-guidance is able to improve in all cases the validity with respect to the new rules, reaching almost 100% validity in all cases. This means that in-distribution conditioning is possible with LTN-guidance. As mentioned previously, the support shift task is more challenging, but LTN-guidance introduces a non-zero likelihood of generating graphs satisfying the rules. Thus, the guidance signal produced by LTN-guidance may be used to produce out-of-distribution samples. sections.heading: 7.4 Limitations
sections.text: LTN-guidance uses a differentiable relaxation of the logical rules, which does not guarantee perfect validity. Another limitation is the requirement for a thorough search for the best guidance weight λ \lambda per dataset. This work tackles the generation of graphs with FOL constraints, on which we found a limited body of competing works and data to compare with. Thus, a broader empirical picture is left for future work.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented how to steer graph denoising diffusion models with FOL rules through LTN-guidance. We first defined a graph signature and consistency axioms under which FOL rules can be written; second, we proposed to interpret the rules as differentiable objective functions through LTN; finally, classifier guidance steers the denoising process with the obtained function. Thus, a pre-trained graph diffusion model can be conditioned to maximize the satisfaction of a set of FOL rules, e.g., the ontology for knowledge graphs. This exact setup has been used to evaluate our technique, showing improved validity compared to the unconditional model. We also studied the behavior during the denoising process, observing that FOL classifier guidance acts aggressively, causing samples to reach their final discrete structure earlier in denoising time. In the future, several diverse graph setups might benefit from its applications. For instance, in counterfactual generation for Graph Neural Networks (GNN) ( Chen et al. 2026 ) one might use LTN-guidance to have control over the counterfactual distribution at inference time. In conditioned molecular generation and retrosynthesis ( Qiao et al. 2025 ) , certain elements may be prohibited, or commercially available starting materials might be required.

sections.heading: Appendix C Knowledge Graphs and Conversion to Labeled Graphs
sections.text: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) ( Hogan et al. 2021 ) are graph-based data representations that cover a variety of data from diverse sources. KGs represent information with nodes being entities of interest and edges being relations between them. This structure allows knowledge to evolve in a flexible manner by enabling granular management of individual entities and relations and allowing missing data. KGs alone only represent data and an ontology may be used to define the schema of the graph, i.e., the types of entities and relations, and the rules they must satisfy. An ontology can be implemented by FOL, starting from the definition of a domain of discourse 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} of entities, and from there defining functions and predicates. The domain is partitioned into subsets 𝒟 1 , … , 𝒟 N {\mathcal{D}}_{1},\dots,{\mathcal{D}}_{N} , each identifying an entity type . A unary predicate P i P_{i} is specified for each subset 𝒟 i {\mathcal{D}}_{i} . The relations set ℛ = { ℛ 1 , … , ℛ M } {\mathcal{R}}=\{{\mathcal{R}}_{1},\dots,{\mathcal{R}}_{M}\} contains subsets ℛ j ⊆ 𝒟 × 𝒟 \mathcal{R}_{j}\subseteq{\mathcal{D}}\times{\mathcal{D}} . A binary predicate R j R_{j} is specified for each relation ℛ j {\mathcal{R}}_{j} . Thus, the triples set becomes 𝒯 = { ( s , r , o ) : s , o ∈ 𝒟 , r ∈ ℛ } . {\mathcal{T}}=\{(s,r,o):s,o\in{\mathcal{D}},r\in{\mathcal{R}}\}. (44) The Resource Description Framework (RDF) ( Cyganiak et al. 2014 ) is a standardized model for representing KGs as a set of triples 𝒯 {\mathcal{T}} , where each triple is of the form ( s , r , o ) (s,r,o) , with s s being the subject entity, r r the edge predicate or relation, and o o the object entity, each represented by an identifier. To define a mapping between KGs in RDF format and labeled graphs, we propose to represent KG entities as node labels, and relations as edge labels. Mathematically, the node labels set is ℒ v = 𝒟 {\mathcal{L}}_{v}={\mathcal{D}} and the edge labels set is ℒ e = ℛ {\mathcal{L}}_{e}={\mathcal{R}} . To convert the triples set 𝒯 {\mathcal{T}} to a labeled graph G G , we first collect the set of unique entities ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ) {\mathcal{L}}({\mathcal{T}}) in 𝒯 {\mathcal{T}} : ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ) \displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}({\mathcal{T}}) = { s ∣ ( s , r , o ) ∈ 𝒯 } ∪ { o ∣ ( s , r , o ) ∈ 𝒯 } . \displaystyle=\{s\mid(s,r,o)\in{\mathcal{T}}\}\cup\{o\mid(s,r,o)\in{\mathcal{T}}\}. (45) Then, we create the vertices 𝒱 {\mathcal{V}} , and couple them to entities with a bijection Λ v \Lambda_{v} : 𝒱 = { v 1 , … , v n } , \displaystyle{\mathcal{V}}=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}, with ​ n = | ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ) | \displaystyle\text{with }n=|{\mathcal{L}}({\mathcal{T}})| (46) Λ v ​ ( v ) = l , \displaystyle\Lambda_{v}(v)=l, v ∈ 𝒱 , l ∈ ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒯 ) . \displaystyle v\in{\mathcal{V}},\ l\in{\mathcal{L}}({\mathcal{T}}). (47) Finally, edges and their labels are defined as: ℰ = { ( v , v ′ ) ∣ v , v ′ ∈ 𝒱 , ( Λ v ( v ) , r , Λ v ( v ′ ) ) ∈ 𝒯 } , \displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}=\{(v,v^{\prime})\mid v,v^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{V}},\ (\Lambda_{v}(v),r,\Lambda_{v}(v^{\prime}))\in{\mathcal{T}}\}, (48) Λ e ​ ( ( v , v ′ ) ) = r , if ​ ( Λ v ​ ( v ) , r , Λ v ​ ( v ′ ) ) ∈ 𝒯 ∧ ( v , v ′ ) ∈ ℰ . \displaystyle\Lambda_{e}((v,v^{\prime}))=r,\quad\text{if}\ (\Lambda_{v}(v),r,\Lambda_{v}(v^{\prime}))\in{\mathcal{T}}\land(v,v^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{E}}. (49) To convert a graph G G to triples 𝒯 {\mathcal{T}} it is enough to collect all edges and labels into the set: 𝒯 = { ( Λ v ​ ( v ) , Λ e ​ ( v , v ′ ) , Λ v ​ ( v ′ ) ) ∣ ( v , v ′ ) ∈ ℰ } . {\mathcal{T}}=\{(\Lambda_{v}(v),\Lambda_{e}(v,v^{\prime}),\Lambda_{v}(v^{\prime}))\mid(v,v^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{E}}\}. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.23766v1 [cs.LG] 16 Oct 2026 Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models Samuel Cognolato Luciano Serafini Alessandro Sperduti Andrea Cavallaro Abstract Graph diffusion models are competitive approaches for generating complex graph-structured data. However, when such distributions have strict structural constraints, diffusion models may fail to capture them exactly, resulting in the generation of invalid graphs. In this paper, we propose a method for grounding graph diffusion models in domain-specific knowledge via First Order Logic (FOL), leveraging its expressive and interpretable formalism to impose structural constraints on the generative process. We incorporate domain knowledge using classifier guidance, a technique that conditions the diffusion model’s distribution on external variables to exert control over the sampled data. During the generative process, classifier guidance steers the denoising trajectory to optimize an objective function, which we define as a fuzzy and differentiable relaxation of the logical rules. Our methodology requires only the specification of constraints in FOL, whose satisfaction is encouraged at inference time to guide a pre-trained generative model. We evaluate our approach by comparing the unconditional generation of knowledge graphs with our logic-guided framework, which incorporates domain ontologies as structural constraints during inference. This approach significantly increases the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy the ontological constraints. 1 Department of Mathematics “Tullio Levi-Civita”, University of Padova, Padova, Italy 2 Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), Trento, Italy 3 Human Inspired Technology Research Centre (HIT), University of Padova, Padova, Italy 4 École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland 1 Introduction Graph generation involves learning an underlying data distribution to facilitate the synthesis of novel, realistic graph structures. Graph diffusion models ( Jo et al. 2022 ; Vignac et al. 2023 ; Huang et al. 2023 ; Cognolato et al. 2026a ; Cognolato et al. 2026b ) and flow-matching models ( Eijkelboom et al. 2024 ; Qin et al. 2024 ) can model distributions over graphs with discrete labels and continuous attributes. In some applications, such as biology, graphs need to satisfy domain-specific rules ( Rigoni et al. 2020 ) that define whether a graph is well-formed. However, neural generative models lack a mechanism to explicitly enforce structural constraints, which requires specialized techniques to tackle them. Thus, the problem of constrained graph generation, i.e., sampling graphs from a subspace of elements satisfying a set of constraints, has gained traction ( Liu et al. 2018 ; Rigoni et al. 2025 ; Madeira et al. 2024 ) . First Order Logic (FOL) ( Barwise 1977 ) may serve as a unified approach to encode and combine heterogeneous constraints. FOL can be used to formalize properties in graphs, where node and edge labels are represented as unary and binary predicates, respectively ( Cai et al. 1992 ) . The rules may act on single nodes, their neighbors, and the type or direction of the relations, e.g., bipartiteness and transitivity. FOL rules may also act considering the whole graph structure, e.g., requiring the presence of a specific node type. The ability to operate both locally and globally provides a tool for controlling the structure and content of graphs. This setup has enabled the definition of ontologies for knowledge graphs, providing a schema for otherwise unstructured data ( Gruber 1993 ) . In this paper, we propose LTN-guidance, a methodology for injecting domain knowledge as FOL constraints into the generative process of graph diffusion models ( Vignac et al. 2023 ) , without any additional training. Our aim is to increase the probability of sampling valid graphs. First, we propose a graph signature, i.e., the collection of symbols defining the vocabulary of the first order language, enabling the definition of logical formulas over labeled graphs. During generation, we use classifier guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol 2021 ) to steer a pre-trained diffusion model toward optimizing rule satisfaction (the external objective function). Our method provides the target FOL constraints as Logic Tensor Network (LTN) ( Badreddine et al. 2022 ) differentiable functions. A mechanism based on Focal Loss ( Lin et al. 2017 ) allows adaptive reweighting of constraints, increasing the contribution of less satisfied sentences in the generative process. Finally, we propose cheaper implementations of LTN functions, e.g., for implementing cardinality constraints over edges. Our main contributions are: 1. A graph signature that allows the definition of logical rules over labeled graphs. We integrate the signature with axioms to ensure label exclusivity; 2. A plug-and-play method for steering graph diffusion models with knowledge in FOL. During inference, FOL constraints are translated to differentiable functions through Logic Tensor Network, and used to steer a pretrained unconditional model with classifier guidance. 3. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first inference-time FOL constraints guidance framework for graph diffusion. 2 Related Work Constrained Graph Generation (CGG) can be based on deep learning or, in the specific case of FOL rules, on Weighted First Order Model Sampling (WFOMS). For deep-learning-based CGG, the application of constraints to deep graph generative models remains in its infancy, as very few works tackle the problem, or are limited to a specific class of constraints. Constrained Graph Variational Auto Encoders (CGVAE) ( Liu et al. 2018 ) and Conditional CGVAE ( Rigoni et al. 2020 ) enforce valency constraints in the molecular domain, closely related to the out-degree of nodes. The model’s generative process is autoregressive, allowing at each step to disable linking with atoms that have filled up their valency. ConStruct ( Madeira et al. 2024 ) is a diffusion model where the whole diffusion and denoising sequences remain in the constrained space, making the samples valid by design. However, the classes of constrains considered are limited to minor-hereditary properties that, if true for a graph, are also true for its minors. The generation of graphs can also be seen as the sampling of variables assignments satisfying the set of FOL rules. This has been explored in Weighted First Order Model Sampling (WFOMS) ( Wang et al. 2024 ) , closely related to Weighted First Order Model Counting (WFOMC) ( Van den Broeck et al. 2011 ) . Lifted (i.e., polynomial) sampling algorithms exist up to the C 2 C^{2} fragment of FOL ( Wang et al. 2024 ) , that is, allowing sentences with universal and counting existential quantifiers ∀ , ∃ ≥ k , ∃ ≤ k , ∃ = k \forall,\exists_{\geq k},\exists_{\leq k},\exists_{=k} with up to two variables per sentence. Although exact in its sampling, lifted WFOMS’s limitation to two variables could render it ineffective for certain applications, such as ontologies with over 3 variables ( Thanapalasingam et al. 2023 ) . Regarding Knowledge Graph (KG) generation, where FOL ontologies are usually defined, there are two prominent KG completion methods: (1) entity embedding and probabilistic link prediction ( Peng et al. 2023 ) ; (2) using Large Language Models (LLM) ( Yao et al. 2025 ) . The former is designed to predict missing links by computing the likelihood of new triples from the trained embeddings and not to generate new entities. The latter treats triples sets as a textual sequence, and new triples are generated as new tokens. However, knowledge graph embedding assumes link independence during sampling, limiting the expressiveness of the resulting graph distributions; at the same time, treating graphs as text negates the inductive biases that facilitate scalability to larger structures. IntelliGraphs contains five Knowledge Graphs (KGs) datasets designed to test different forms of semantic validity. syn-paths tests directed path structure; syn-types tests compatibility between entity and relation types together with a fixed-cardinality constraint; and syn-tipr instantiates a time-indexed person-role ontology pattern. The two real-world datasets contain Wikidata-derived subgraphs: wd-movies describes a movie through actors, directors, and genres, whereas wd-articles describes scholarly articles and ordered authorship information. The latter is the most structurally complex because valid graphs must represent consecutive author positions without gaps. This same benchmark was used in Wang et al. (2025) , and the amount of available data is substantially larger than existing generic graph datasets ( Huang et al. 2023 ) . In syn-types and wd-movies , we observe that unconditional DiGress is outperformed by the ProvCreator baseline. For the former, we find that the source of error is the cardinality constraint of the dataset. In fact, the validity reached by DiGress is very close to the percentage of triples set of length 10 without duplicates in the dataset. The inclusion of the cardinality constraint in Eq. 24 improves its satisfaction, leading to the very high validity of 95.70 % 95.70\% . In wd-movies , LTN-guidance also improves results over vanilla DiGress with an average validity of 97.37 % 97.37\% , outperforming ProvCreator. Still, classifier guidance did not show substantial improvements on wd-articles , the most challenging dataset. In particular, the most unsatisfied constraint entails having no gaps in the paper author positions. Near the final denoising steps, the unconditional transition becomes sharply concentrated, and the chosen guidance strength is insufficient to change the model’s predictions. Increasing the weights was insufficient, so a more complex weighting scheme is needed. Regarding distributional metrics, we observe that guidance does not substantially skew the distribution compared to the unconditional models. This means that the technique does not sacrifice sample quality for validity.
